title: Moses' excuses (Exodus 4:10–17)
hook: I'm slow of speech; send someone else, please
carry: I will be with your mouth

segments.voice: Yesterday, a name that is a verb: I am that I am, four letters printed LORD. What did you notice after your own I am? Day three hundred eighty-three.

Everyone has a reason not to. I'm not qualified. I'm not ready. Someone else would be better at this. I'll do it when things calm down. At the burning bush, Moses runs through the whole list. First: who am I, to go to Pharaoh? God says, I will be with you. Second: what's your name? God answers, I AM. Third: what if they don't believe me? God gives him signs, a staff that turns into a snake, a hand that turns white and back. You'd think that would settle it. A talking fire, a new name for God, miracles on demand. But Moses has two more excuses left.
screen: `WHO AM I?` → `WHAT IS YOUR NAME?` → `THEY WON'T BELIEVE ME.`

segments.voice: The fourth, in the King James Bible: "O my Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue." In Hebrew, heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue. Nobody knows exactly what that means. Some readers think Moses had a stammer. Some think he'd lost his Egyptian after years in the desert. A later Jewish story tells of the baby Moses burning his tongue on a coal in Pharaoh's palace. The Bible itself just says heavy. And God answers with a question: "Who hath made man's mouth?" Then the promise that gives us today's line: "Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say." Not, I'll fix your mouth. I'll be with it. And then the fifth excuse, the honest one, stripped of reasons: "O my Lord, send, I pray thee, by the hand of him whom thou wilt send." Send someone else. Please. That's when, the text says, God's anger burns. And yet God still doesn't give up on him. Your brother Aaron, God says. I know he can speak well. He's already on his way to meet you. He'll be your mouth, and I'll be with both your mouths. And take the staff. So the reluctant one goes, with help. Christians have taken comfort here for centuries. Paul writes that God chose the weak things of the world. Prophets after Moses protest that they're too young or too sinful. The Bible's leaders keep beginning with I can't, and keep being told, I will be with you.
screen: `HEAVY OF MOUTH, HEAVY OF TONGUE.` · `WHO HATH MADE MAN'S MOUTH?` · `SEND SOMEONE ELSE.` · `AARON WILL SPEAK WITH YOU.` · then, large: `I WILL BE WITH THY MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice your favorite excuse. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been asked to do, or feel pulled toward, that you keep avoiding. Now listen for the excuse you reach for. Not qualified? Not the right time? Someone else would do it better? Name it. Don't argue with it. Just hear it clearly, the way Moses finally said it plainly: send someone else. Then ask who your Aaron might be, the help you haven't asked for. If you pray, you can bring both to God. The bell holds the time.
Moses' excuses. Five reasons Moses gave at the burning bush not to go, ending with the plainest one: please send someone else.
Your line: I will be with your mouth. Today, say the thing you've been afraid to say, even clumsily, and let it be enough. Day three hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Many Christians return to Moses's excuses when they feel called to something and inadequate for it, and churches often use Exodus 4 when encouraging people who are nervous about speaking, teaching or serving.

fork.setup: you're Moses. you've had a talking fire, a new name for God, and miracles in your own hands. you're still terrified. what do you say?
options: let me think about it for a year.
fork.reveal: "send, I pray thee, by the hand of him whom thou wilt send." God's anger burns, but God sends Aaron to help, and Moses goes.

original.note: Hebrew: heavy of mouth. Moses's phrase for his speech, which the KJV gives as slow of speech.

trapdoor: what you thought: Moses was a born leader and a great speaker.
what it means: he gave five excuses, ending with send someone else, and went only with a promise and a brother.
what a scholar hears: kevad peh, heavy of mouth, may mean a speech difficulty or simply lack of eloquence; later Jewish tradition told a story about a coal to explain it.

notes: The coal story is from Exodus Rabbah 1:26 (a later midrash); presented as 'a later Jewish story'. Confirm citation.
The five objections (3:11, 3:13, 4:1, 4:10, 4:13) are a common way of counting; confirm.
Prophets protesting (Jeremiah 1:6 too young; Isaiah 6:5 unclean lips) and 1 Corinthians 1:27 paraphrased.
Aaron 'already on his way' paraphrases 4:14 ('he cometh forth to meet thee').
